skills.name: jump
skills.description_text: Jumps require you to use both feet to hit two or more notes at the same time. This can take a lot of energy, so it is valuable to learn how to conserve energy on jumps. At fast NPS, jumps can alternatively be executed as a run, at double time rhythm.

skills.name: drill
skills.description_text: Drills are a series of notes (here, defined as 5 or more notes) that alternate between just two panels. Compared to runs at the same level, drills can demand higher speeds and length because in principle you can conserve much more energy on drills. Most players find blue-panel drills executed with heels much easier than red-panel drills that require toes, to the extent that some players even position their feet to perform red drills with their heels.

skills.name: run
skills.description_text: Runs, or streams, are a series of notes (here, defined as 7 or more notes) at constant rhythm. Unlike drills which alternate between just two panels, runs involve a variety of panels, which in doubles can require you to move around the pads. In most arcade-length charts, the crux is an ending run, between 5 seconds to 25 seconds long. 8th note runs at 100 BPM to 200 BPM correspond to 3.3 notes per second (NPS) to ~6.7 NPS and are found at S6S14. 16th note runs at 100 BPM to 200+ BPM, or ~6.7 NPS to ~13.3+ NPS start to be introduced at S16 and beyond.

skills.name: run without twists
skills.description_text: Runs without twists are the most straightforward type of run. For a given difficulty level, these are longer in duration than full runs, which make them a useful stepping stone for improving at runs and improving time under tension.

skills.name: twist over90
skills.description_text: A twist at >90 degrees involves hitting panels at greater than 90 degree angle. Compared to the base stance where your body faces the screen, during a >90 degree twist, you step with one foot fully crossing the other foot, so that your body or hips twist beyond being perpendicular to the screen.

skills.name: side3 singles
skills.description_text: Side3 singles describes chart sections that primarily use the side 3 arrows in singles. Twists in these sections are sometimes called corner twists.

skills.name: mid6 doubles
skills.description_text: Mid6 doubles, also known as half-doubles, describes chart sections that primarily use the middle 6 panels in doubles. Strong familiarity with mid6 double patterns are necessary for advancing in doubles beyond a certain level. Half-double patterns can sometimes be the hardest part of learning doubles after learning singles.

skills.name: mid4 doubles

skills.name: doublestep
skills.description_text: Doublestepping is stepping with the same foot twice in a row, contrasting with the typical flow of alternating feet. Doublestepping is primarily forced in stepcharts by requiring one foot remain on a hold, while the other foot hits multiple arrows in a row. Unlike jacks where you hit the same panel, doublestepping hits different panels.

skills.name: jack
skills.description_text: Jacks are when you execute a pattern of multiple arrows in a row on the same panel, by using one foot to hit all the arrows. To properly execute jacks, it is important to completely lift your foot off the panel each time, which can be a common mistake at higher speeds. Jacks are related to footswitches, where repeated arrows are instead hit with alternating feet.

skills.name: footswitch
skills.description_text: Footswitches are when you execute a pattern of multiple arrows in a row on the same panel, by alternating feet. These are an alternative to jacks, where the correct choice depends on the chart context. Typically, footswitches are the correct answer with irregular rhythm, or when they avoid a difficult twist forced with jacks.

skills.name: bracket
skills.description_text: A bracket is hitting two arrows with one foot at the same time. Brackets require the two arrows to be physically next to each other on the pad.

skills.name: staggered bracket
skills.description_text: A staggered bracket are two arrows close in time, but not at the same time, which are nevertheless executed as a bracket with one foot. The perfect judgment window in Pump on normal judgment is 83.2 milliseconds after a note, so consecutive notes at speeds faster than 12.02 NPS can be staggered-bracketed.
